generated_summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a pathogen that causes serious respiratory, blood, liver, and bladder infections. This bacterium is a significant clinical concern because it causes life-threatening diseases like pneumonia. The adaptor protein SKAP2 is required for protection against K. pneumoniae pulmonary infections. Researchers studied how this specific protein helps the body defend against lung infections. Mice lacking SKAP2 had 100-fold higher bacterial burden compared to wild-type mice. SKAP2 expression in innate immune cells controlled the amount of bacteria in the lungs. K. pneumoniae-stimulated reactive oxygen species production was abolished in neutrophils lacking SKAP2. These neutrophils degranulated normally but could not produce the chemicals needed to kill bacteria. The neutrophil ROS response required the activity of SFKs, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and PKC. These specific proteins must work together to trigger the production of reactive oxygen species. The loss of SKAP2 hindered the K. pneumoniae-induced phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2. SKAP2 is proximal to their activation within the signaling pathways used to fight pathogens. SKAP2-dependent signaling in neutrophils is essential for K. pneumoniae-activated ROS production. This signaling process is also necessary for promoting bacterial clearance during an infection.

generated_summary: Plasmodium vivax malaria causes relapse infections when dormant parasites activate in the liver. These dormant parasites, called hypnozoites, cause new blood infections weeks or months later. Researchers developed a mathematical model to track these liver-stage hypnozoites within a host. The team validated this model using data from tropical strains of the P. vivax parasite. This model shows how the hypnozoite reservoir builds up after new infections occur. The reservoir then depletes as the parasites either activate or die over time. The model predicts that the hypnozoite reservoir is over-dispersed among the population. Many people have few parasites, while some individuals have intensely infected livers. Individuals with more hypnozoites are predicted to experience more frequent malaria relapses. These heavily infected individuals also contribute more to onwards P. vivax transmission. Using hypnozoite-killing drugs like primaquine in first-line treatment can reduce disease spread. This strategy targets individuals most likely to relapse and spread the infection further. A higher number of hypnozoites is associated with a shorter time to first relapse. The model assumes that each hypnozoite activates and dies at a constant rate. The within-host model was integrated into a larger P. vivax transmission model. This integration allows researchers to simulate parasite movement between humans and mosquitoes.

generated_summary: Selective logging in Amazonian forests disturbs 2 Mha annually and emits 90 Tg of carbon. This logging involves harvesting specific tree species and releases carbon into the atmosphere. Forest regrowth can counterbalance the carbon emissions resulting from selective logging. Selectively logged forests often remain forested and can recover their stored carbon over time. Researchers used an original modeling approach calibrated on 133 permanent forest plots across Amazonia. The model provides Amazon-wide predictions of post-logging C recovery using long-term inventory data. Net aboveground C recovery over 10 years is higher in the Guiana Shield and western Amazon. These regions recover 21 ±3 Mg C ha-1 compared to 12 ±3 Mg C ha-1 in the south. The southern Amazon shows lower recovery because environmental stress in that region is high. High environmental stress includes factors like low rainfall and high seasonality in the south. The study highlights the key role of survivors in the forest regrowth process. Trees that survive logging contribute the most to carbon recovery across the entire Amazon. Researchers elaborated a comprehensive map of post-disturbance C recovery potential in Amazonia. This map helps identify where forests have the highest potential to regain lost carbon.

generated_summary: Many decisions are thought to arise from the accumulation of noisy evidence until a threshold is reached. This model suggests that the brain gathers information over time until enough evidence crosses a certain point. The bounded evidence accumulation theory predicts that an increase in noise should lead to faster decisions. This theory also predicts that more noise leads to reduced accuracy and paradoxically higher confidence. Researchers developed a novel sensory manipulation to mimic unbiased noise in motion-selective visual cortex regions. The researchers verified this method using neuronal recordings in macaque areas MT/MST. In both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence. These effects occurred over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired. The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model. This suggests the model accurately describes how the brain processes noisy information to make decisions. Increasing noise accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable nearer to the termination bounds. This acceleration explains why the reaction time becomes faster when volatility increases. The team used a random dot motion display to manipulate motion information. They added a second level of randomness which increased volatility without biasing the motion direction. High volatility decreased reaction times particularly at the weakest motion strengths. The manipulation affected accuracy only subtly and was not statistically reliable for individual subjects. The framework accounts for the joint effect of volatility on choice and reaction time.

generated_summary: The insulin-like signaling pathway keeps the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans short by inactivating DAF-16. DAF-16 is a protein in these worms similar to human FOXO transcription factors. The enzyme Calcineurin also limits the lifespan of C. elegans through an unknown mechanism. Calcineurin is a type of protein known as a PP2B phosphatase. Researchers found that TAX-6•CNB-1 and UNC-43 regulate worm lifespan by acting on DAF-16. TAX-6•CNB-1 is the worm version of Calcineurin and UNC-43 is the version of CAMKII. UNC-43 regulates DAF-16 when the worms face starvation, heat, or oxidative stress. This protein works together with insulin signaling to control how long the worms live. Unlike insulin signaling, UNC-43 phosphorylates and activates DAF-16 to promote its nuclear localization. This activation causes the DAF-16 protein to move into the nucleus of the cell. TAX-6•CNB-1 removes the phosphorylation of DAF-16 at S286, which leads to DAF-16 inactivation. Removing this specific phosphate group stops the activity of the DAF-16 protein. The mammalian protein FOXO3 is also regulated by CAMKIIA and Calcineurin. This regulatory mechanism is not unique to worms. Mammalian CAMKII and Calcineurin regulate FOXO3 at a conserved site. This suggests that the lifespan control mechanism is similar in more complex animals.

A mutant protein lacking the transactivation domain failed to fix nerve defects. This result shows that transcription regulation is necessary for nerve development. The cell-adhesion function of β-Catenin is not needed for this process. This finding helps narrow down how the protein works in muscle cells. The study identified Slit2 as a protein directed by muscle β-Catenin. Slit2 acts as a retrograde factor that sends signals back to nerves. Slit2 immobilized on beads induced synaptophysin puncta in spinal cord axons. These puncta are markers that show where new nerve connections form. Slit2 serves as a factor used by muscle β-Catenin to guide nerves. This mechanism ensures that muscles and nerves connect correctly during development.

generated_summary: In Arabidopsis thaliana, 24 nt siRNA molecules guide the silencing of transposons and specific genes. These small RNAs help add chemical tags to DNA through a process called cytosine methylation. The biogenesis of 24 nt siRNA requires Pol IV, RDR2, and the enzyme DCL3. These proteins work together in the cell nucleus to produce the small silencing RNAs. The specific RNA molecules that serve as siRNA precursors were previously mostly undefined. Researchers needed to identify the longer RNA strands that DCL3 cuts into smaller pieces. The study identified P4R2 RNAs that accumulate in dcl3 mutants and are diced by DCL3. In laboratory tests, DCL3 successfully cut these P4R2 RNAs into 24 nt RNAs. Most P4R2 RNAs are 26-45 nt long and start with a purine next to a pyrimidine. These physical traits match the characteristics of Pol IV transcripts generated in vitro. RDR2 terminal transferase activity explains occasional non-templated nucleotides at P4R2 RNA 3’ termini. This activity allows the RDR2 enzyme to add extra bases to the end of the RNA. The 24 nt siRNAs primarily correspond to the 5’ or 3’ ends of P4R2 RNAs. This pattern suggests that siRNAs are generated from either end by single dicing events.

generated_summary: The bacterium Shigella flexneri produces an enzyme called OspI that modifies host proteins. OspI deamidates a glutamine residue in the host enzyme UBC13, converting it to glutamate. Deamidation of UBC13 by OspI silences its polyubiquitination activity in complex with TRAF6. This silencing of the complex also stops the downstream NF-κB inflammatory response. The precise role of deamidation in silencing the UBC13/TRAF6 complex was previously unknown. Researchers wanted to understand how this modification prevents the two proteins from working together. Deamidation inhibits the interaction between UBC13 and the TRAF6 RING-domain. The modification perturbs both the stable native interactions and the temporary transient interactions. Deamidation creates a new intramolecular salt-bridge within the UBC13 protein. This internal bond competes with a critical intermolecular salt-bridge at the UBC13/TRAF6RING interface. The salt-bridge competition prevents transient interactions necessary to form a typical UBC13/RING complex. These fleeting contacts are essential for the two proteins to bind correctly. Repulsion between E100 and the negatively charged surface of RING also prevents transient interactions. The negative charge of the new glutamate pushes away the TRAF6 RING-domain surface. These findings highlight a mechanism where a post-translational modification inhibits protein-protein association. The modification perturbs the conformation and stability of transient complexes to block binding.

generated_summary: Bacteriophages are viruses that use a receptor binding protein to interact with host bacteria. This receptor binding protein is often called the RBP for short. The molecular rules governing RBP function and host range are not well understood. Host range refers to the specific types of bacteria a phage can infect. Researchers developed a high-throughput engineering method to create 1660 variants of the T7 phage RBP. This method allowed them to study every individual residue in the RBP tip domain. The study identified several previously unknown regions of functional importance within the T7 phage RBP. These regions were found by comparing how different variants performed across various hosts. Substitution patterns showed host-specific differences in the position and properties of mutations. These patterns reveal how the phage adapts at a molecular level to individual hosts. The researchers discovered gain-of-function variants that could infect bacteria normally resistant to the phage. They also found host-constricting variants that eliminated only specific types of bacteria. Highly active T7 variants were engineered against a pathogen that causes urinary tract infections. This work demonstrates the therapeutic utility of engineering phages to fight specific diseases. The approach provides a generalized framework for characterizing sequence-function relationships in phage-bacterial systems. This framework can be applied to many different types of viruses and bacteria.

generated_summary: Devil Facial Tumour 2 is a recently discovered contagious cancer in Tasmanian devils. Tasmanian devils already suffer from another widespread contagious cancer called Devil Facial Tumour 1. Unlike the first cancer, Devil Facial Tumour 2 cells express MHC class I molecules. This similarity reduces the ability of the host immune system to trigger a response. Some of these molecules are non-polymorphic, meaning they do not vary between individuals. Losing these specific markers allows the cancer to hide from almost any host devil.

SpoIVA evolved from a TRAFAC class of P-loop GTPases. This means the protein originally came from a family that used GTP instead of ATP. generated_summary: Leptin is a hormone that regulates energy balance and brain development during growth. This hormone has neurotrophic effects that help shape the nervous system. The specific role of leptin during early development is not yet fully understood. Researchers want to know which effects of the hormone are permanent or reversible. Scientists studied mice that lacked the leptin receptor gene from birth. They restored leptin signaling at either the fourth or tenth week of age. Some brain defects thought to be permanent were recovered by restoring the receptor. This recovery included the growth of neural projections in the arcuate nucleus. However, lacking the receptor in early life led to irreversible obesity in mice. This weight gain happened because the body suppressed its energy expenditure. Restoring the receptor in adulthood did not fix certain gene expression levels. The mice still showed defects in the reproductive system and brain growth. Early defects in leptin signaling cause permanent metabolic and developmental problems. These findings show that early life is a critical window for hormone action. Adult receptor reactivation caused a persistent reduction in hypothalamic Pomc and Cartpt expression. The levels of Prlh mRNA expression also remained lower in the hypothalamus.

generated_summary: In social settings, speech waveforms from nearby speakers mix together in our ear canals. When multiple people speak at once, their speech sounds combine before reaching our ears. The brain normally unmixes attended speech from background speakers using fast temporal processing. The brain also uses cognitive active listening mechanisms to separate one person's speech. Approximately 10% of adults visiting the clinic for reduced hearing have clinically normal hearing. Standard clinical tests often fail to capture real world communication difficulties in these adults. Multi-talker speech intelligibility thresholds varied widely in adults with normal hearing. These thresholds were predicted from neural phase-locking to frequency modulation cues using EEG. Combining neural temporal fine structure processing and pupil-indexed listening effort explained most differences. These factors and behavioral FM thresholds accounted for 78% of the variability in intelligibility. The identified markers of poor multi-talker speech perception could inform next-generation clinical tests. These tests could help identify hidden hearing disorders that standard exams currently miss. Low-cost EEG systems and pupillometry cameras could provide objective measures for perceptual difficulties. These tools could provide hearing health providers with readouts for therapeutic drugs or devices.

generated_summary: Most actin-like proteins form filaments from two strands that run in the same direction. This parallel arrangement creates a clear direction or polarity for the protein filament. The bacterial protein MreB forms pairs of strands that face in opposite directions. This antiparallel arrangement occurs both inside living cells and in laboratory tests. Researchers used crystal structures to see these opposite strands at an atomic level. These structures specifically showed the arrangement of MreB from the bacterium Caulobacter. The double strand is essential for MreB to maintain the shape of cells. Without this structure, bacterial cells cannot keep their correct physical form. Advanced imaging shows that these MreB pairs bind tightly to cell membranes. The 3D cryo-EM technique confirmed this strong attachment in Caulobacter bacteria. MreB undergoes specific shape changes when forming these opposite-facing filaments. Small structural changes trigger the assembly of these protein strands into filaments. Antimicrobial agents like A22 bind to MreB and destabilize the double strands. This binding likely stops the energy process needed for the protein to function. Tests in E. coli bacteria confirmed the same opposite orientation of the strands. The researchers used site-specific cross-linking to verify this orientation in living cells.

generated_summary: Arabidopsis thaliana flowers consistently produce four petals in every bloom. This stable petal number is an invariant and robust trait. The closely related species Cardamine hirsuta exhibits a variable petal number. The genetic basis for this difference between species was previously unknown. Divergence in the floral regulator APETALA1 explains the difference in robustness. This gene, also called AP1, controls how petals form during development. Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 confers robustness by masking specific genetic loci. It hides the effects of quantitative trait loci that cause variation. Cardamine hirsuta AP1 fails to complement the function of the Arabidopsis version. Upstream regulatory regions of the gene contribute to this functional divergence. Variable petal number persists in Cardamine hirsuta despite available genetic variation. Natural populations have enough variation to potentially produce four-petalled flowers. The Arabidopsis version of the gene uses epistatic interactions to ensure stability. These interactions prevent other genes from changing the final petal count. The study identified AP1 as a major factor in floral evolution. It determines if a species has a fixed or variable phenotype. Cardamine hirsuta flowers display between zero and four petals on one plant. This variation occurs even though the species is closely related to Arabidopsis.

We mapped this natural variation to specific QTL in the C . hirsuta genome and showed that introducing the A . thaliana AP1 locus masked the effects of all QTL . generated_summary: SUV39H is a primary enzyme that adds methyl groups to histone H3 lysine 9. This modification is essential for forming a tightly packed form of DNA called heterochromatin. SUV39H recognizes trimethylated H3K9 through its chromodomain to target specific chromosomal regions. The chromodomain acts as a module that helps the enzyme find its correct location. The mechanisms by which SUV39H targets naïve chromatin without existing H3K9me3 are poorly understood. Naïve chromatin refers to DNA that has not yet received these specific chemical marks. The chromodomain of Suv39h1 binds to nucleic acids to help assemble heterochromatin. Suv39h1 is the specific version of this enzyme found in mouse cells. The Suv39h1 chromodomain has a higher binding affinity for RNA than for DNA. This nucleic acid binding is independent of how the enzyme recognizes H3K9me3 marks. Suv39h1 binds to major satellite RNAs in living organisms to stay on the pericentromere. Reducing these specific RNAs lowers the retention of the enzyme on the chromosome. Both nucleic acid-binding and H3K9me-binding activities are crucial for pericentric heterochromatin assembly. Mutational studies confirmed that the enzyme needs both functions to work properly. Chromatin-bound RNAs contribute to creating the target specificity of the SUV39H enzyme. These RNA molecules help guide the enzyme to its specific targets on the chromosomes.

generated_summary: Grid cells in the entorhinal cortex allow for the precise decoding of position in space. These specialized brain cells help animals understand their exact location within an environment. Grid cells have recently been hypothesized to make a general contribution to mental operations. This idea suggests these cells support cognitive functions beyond just physical navigation. A prerequisite for this hypothesis is that grid cell activity does not critically depend on physical movement. The cells must be able to function even when the body is not moving. Movement of covert attention without any physical movement elicits spatial receptive fields with triangular tiling. This triangular tiling of space is a hallmark pattern of grid cell activity. Researchers identified a significant population of entorhinal cells in monkeys that had spatially structured receptive fields. About 14% of the 141 recorded neurons showed these patterns while the monkeys focused attention. Grid-like representations were not observed in recordings obtained from the hippocampus in this study. The lack of these patterns in the hippocampus highlights the unique role of the entorhinal cortex. The results provide evidence that neurons in the macaque entorhinal cortex do not rely on physical movement. These neurons can represent the location of attention even when the eyes and body remain still.

generated_summary: Bacteriophage BPP-1 is a virus that infects and kills bacteria causing whooping cough. These bacteria belong to the Bordetella species which cause respiratory illness. BPP-1 has a diversity-generating retroelement (DGR) that acts as a phage-display system. Engineering efforts were hampered because the virus lacked known atomic structures. Researchers used cryo electron microscopy to view the BPP-1 head structure. This method provided a detailed view at a 3.5 Å resolution. The atomic model shows the cement protein (CP) has a jellyroll fold. The major capsid protein (MCP) has an HK97-like fold called a Johnson fold. The fold topology of MCP is permuted non-circularly from the Johnson fold topology. This specific arrangement is different from previously observed viral and cellular proteins. Electrostatic interactions and β-sheet augmentation form a non-covalent chainmail in BPP-1. This differs from the covalent inter-protein linkages found in the HK97 chainmail. The termini of CP and MCP are ideally positioned for DGR-based phage-display engineering. These protein ends are exposed on the surface to display peptide libraries. BPP-1 is the first virus shown to contain both jellyroll and HK97-like folds. Most viruses belong to lineages with only one characteristic fold in their proteins. The new topology is likely the only feasible alternative to the old topology. Strong electrostatic interactions between adjacent proteins stabilize the BPP-1 chainmail structure.

Proteomics of isolated lysosomes identified GLMP as an accessory subunit. GLMP acts as a critical partner for the MFSD1 protein. The MFSD1 and GLMP proteins physically interact with each other. This physical interaction suggests the two proteins work together closely. GLMP is essential for maintaining normal levels of MFSD1 in lysosomes. GLMP protects the MFSD1 protein from being broken down by proteolysis. Glmp knockout mice mimic the phenotype of Mfsd1 knockout mice. feedback_items.fact: Inactivation of Meis1 in mouse neural crest leads to an altered sympatho-vagal regulation of cardiac rhythmicity in adults, characterized by chronotropic incompetence and cardiac conduction defects, increasing susceptibility to sudden cardiac death (SCD).

feedback_items.source_span: Here we analyze a new mouse missense variant , Rasgrp1Anaef , with an ENU-mutated EF hand in the Rasgrp1 Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor . The mutant codon , located in Rasgrp1’s second EF hand ( EF2 ) , encodes a neutral amino acid glycine ( G ) instead of the normal arginine ( R ) , a large polar molecule with a positive charge ( Rasgrp1 R519G; Figure 2A , B ) . The ENU-generated allele was named ‘Rasgrp1Anaef’ to reflect the combination of antinuclear antibody ( ANA ) production and the amino acid substitution in the EF hand .

feedback_items.source_span: We show that elimination of this interaction by either removal of Munc13 or replacement of Munc13 with a Munc13 C2B mutant alters synaptic VGCC's response to and recovery from high-frequency action potential bursts and alters calcium influx from single action potential stimuli . We show that elimination of this interaction by either removal of Munc13 or replacement of Munc13 with a Munc13 C2B mutant alters synaptic VGCC's response to and recovery from high-frequency action potential bursts and alters calcium influx from single action potential stimuli . Loss of Munc13 at hippocampal nerve terminals profoundly alters the response of VGCCs during brief AP bursts of very high-frequency firing .

generated_summary: Many plants have puzzle-shaped cells in their outer layer called the epidermis. The functional benefit of these complex cell shapes has remained elusive. These intricate forms may provide a strategy to reduce mechanical stress. This reduction in stress occurs specifically within the cell wall. Lobes emerge when tissue-level growth is isotropic or uniform in all directions. These lobes prevent large isodiametric cells from bulging under internal turgor pressure. Data from various plant organs and species support this growth isotropy relationship. The researchers tested this by using mutants where growth direction was perturbed. Simulation models show that actively regulating cellular stress reproduces the cell shape. These models mimic the development of the epidermal cell shape. Reducing stress potentially lowers the amount of material required for cell walls. The cell wall maintains mechanical integrity with less cellulose and other materials. Organs with uniform growth have puzzle shapes while elongated organs have fewer lobes. Genetic changes that modify growth anisotropy result in the predicted cell shapes.

feedback_items.source_span: Extracellular Hedgehog ( Hh ) proteins induce transcriptional changes in target cells by inhibiting the proteolytic processing of full-length Drosophila Ci or mammalian Gli proteins to nuclear transcriptional repressors and by activating the full-length Ci or Gli proteins . Hh controls Ci activity by regulating the processing , activation , and degradation of full-length Ci ( known as Ci-155 ) .

generated_summary: Researchers must clarify neuronal circuits in the spinal cord dorsal horn to understand pathological pain. The spinal cord dorsal horn is a critical area for processing sensory perception. This study used an optogenetic approach to selectively activate spinal interneurons expressing calretinin. Calretinin is a calcium-binding protein found in specific types of nerve cells. Calretinin interneurons form an interconnected network that can initiate and sustain excitatory signaling. This network allows the spinal cord to boost and prolong sensory signals. These calretinin interneurons directly relay signals to lamina I projection neurons. Projection neurons are responsible for sending sensory information from the spinal cord to the brain. Photoactivation of calretinin interneurons in vivo resulted in significant nocifensive behavior. Higher sensory thresholds mean the animals were less sensitive to touch or pain stimuli. Dorsal horn circuits involving excitatory calretinin neurons are important for the amplification of pain. These circuits can increase pain signals even without a new injury to the body. Calretinin interneurons are identified as a future analgesic target for pain relief. generated_summary: Mutations in the RAB23 gene cause a condition called Carpenter Syndrome. This syndrome involves developmental problems like extra digits and skull morphogenesis defects. Researchers generated Rab23-deficient mice to study how this protein regulates skull development. These mice survived long enough to allow the study of skeletal development. The Rab23-deficient mice showed premature fusion of multiple sutures in the skull. This fusion, known as craniosynostosis, results from abnormal growth of bone-forming cells. In Rab23-deficient sutures, FGF10-driven FGFR1 signaling is significantly elevated. This change causes an imbalance in MAPK and Hedgehog signaling pathways. feedback_items.source_span: However , it remains unclear whether this inheritance can direct long-term memory of individual gene expression states ( cis memory ) or instead if local chromatin states are dictated by the concentrations of diffusible factors ( trans memory ) . While in both trans and cis memory the chromatin state is inherited , in the former case chromatin responds to the transcriptional state defined by heritable concentrations of the trans-factors , whereas in the latter case it is the local chromatin environment that instructs its own inheritance and is , therefore , the key epigenetic memory element . If FLC transcriptional states are defined by concentrations of diffusible factors ( trans memory ) , then all copies of FLC within a cell should be in the same transcriptional state .

Asymptomatic carriage in the nasopharynx is a necessary prerequisite for this disease to occur.
The bacteria live in the nose without causing symptoms before they spread.
Researchers developed a model to calculate the duration of carriage episodes from swab data.
The study analyzed data from 598 unvaccinated children over a two year period.
Pneumococcal genomic variation accounted for 63% of the variation in carriage duration.
Host traits like age and previous carriage accounted for less than 5%.
The study quantified how serotype and drug-resistance affect the duration of carriage.
Serotype explained 17% of the variation while drug-resistance explained 9%.
Specific prophage sequences were linked to decreased carriage duration independent of serotype.
This effect may occur through the disruption of the bacterial competence mechanism.
These findings support theoretical models of pneumococcal competition and antibiotic resistance.
The results help explain how different bacterial strains compete within the human host.
Longer carriage duration increases the likelihood of transmission to another person.

Other significant locus effects accounted for 7% of the variation in carriage duration.

feedback_items.fact: The duration of Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage episodes was calculated using a new model developed from longitudinal swab data.
feedback_items.source_span: Here we developed a model to calculate the duration of carriage episodes from longitudinal swab data , and combined these results with whole genome sequence data . By developing models for longitudinal swab data and combining the results with whole genome sequence data we have quantified and mapped the genetic contribution to the carriage duration of S . pneumoniae . For 598 unvaccinated children up to 24 swabs taken over a two year period were available , an extension on the previous study ( Turner et al . , 2012 , 2013a ) . To estimate carriage duration from the longitudinal swab data we constructed a set of hidden Markov models ( HMMs ) with hidden states corresponding to whether a child was carrying a serotype at a given time point , and observed states corresponding to whether a positive swab was observed for this serotype at this time point .

generated_summary: The study investigated how protein mobility depends on protein surface properties and ionic strength. Protein mobility refers to how fast proteins move within the fluid of a cell. Researchers used surface-modified fluorescent proteins to determine translational diffusion coefficients in three different organisms. These organisms included Escherichia coli, Lactococcus lactis, and the archaeon Haloferax volcanii. In E. coli, the diffusion coefficient depends on the net charge and its distribution. Positive proteins moved up to 100-fold slower than negative ones in this bacterium. The effect of protein charge on diffusion is weaker in L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii. This difference occurs because electrostatic screening reduces the electrical interactions in these species. The decrease in mobility is likely caused by the interaction of positive proteins with ribosomes. This interaction was shown in vivo and confirmed in vitro with purified ribosomes. Ribosome surface properties may thus limit the composition of the cytoplasmic proteome. The cytoplasmic proteome is the entire set of proteins found within the cell fluid. Applying these findings to prokaryotic (endo)symbionts reveals a paradox in how these cells function. It remains unclear how these specific organisms avoid slow diffusion and ribosome swarming.

generated_summary: The biological mechanisms that activate regeneration in animals remain mysterious. Scientists want to understand how bodies know when to start regrowing. Planarians show distinct molecular responses to wounds that involve tissue absence. These flatworms can regenerate their entire bodies after a major injury. The study identified Smed-follistatin as a gene required for planarian regeneration. This gene is a follistatin homolog found in the flatworm species. Smed-follistatin inhibition blocks the specific responses to tissue absence in planarians. However, blocking this gene does not prevent normal tissue turnover. Two activin homologs are required for the Smed-follistatin phenotype to occur. These proteins are named Smed-activin-1 and Smed-activin-2. Smed-follistatin expression is wound-induced and higher after injuries with tissue absence. The amount of the gene increases when tissue is actually lost. Smed-follistatin inhibits Smed-Activin proteins to trigger regeneration after tissue loss. This interaction identifies a critical mechanism for regeneration initiation. The requirement for the gene is specific to replacing lost tissue. Normal cell replacement continues even when the gene is not active. Planarians mount different reactions depending on whether an injury causes tissue loss. The flatworms distinguish between simple wounds and those requiring major regrowth.

generated_summary: Opioid overdose rates in the United States quadrupled between 1999 and 2017. These rising rates led to a staggering 130 deaths per day. Finding brain areas and cell types involved in breathing depression is necessary. Opioid-induced respiratory depression causes slow and shallow breathing during an overdose. Researchers identified two primary changes to murine breathing after administering opioids. These changes include decreased inspiratory airflow and a new pause phase. The researchers confirmed these changes by locally eliminating the µ-Opioid receptor. This receptor is the protein that opioids attach to in the brain. The preBötzinger Complex is the critical brain site for opioid sensitivity. This specific brainstem region is where the breathing rhythm originates. Just 70–140 neurons in the preBötzinger Complex cause this opioid sensitivity. Genetic tools helped reveal this very small number of responsible cells. Characterizing these neurons may lead to therapies that prevent respiratory depression. These new treatments could stop breathing failure while still sparing analgesia. These critical neurons are not required for opioid-induced pain relief. This finding suggests a target for developing much safer opioid drugs. The pause phase delays the initiation of subsequent breaths in mice. Researchers monitored breathing closely after exposing the animals to opioids. Scientists used stereotaxic injection to eliminate receptors from specific cells. This method targeted the brainstem circuitry while sparing other inputs.

The protein ensures that visual circuits function correctly as the environment changes.

generated_summary: Drosophila neural progenitors, called neuroblasts, are a good model for studying how brain stem cells renew themselves. These neuroblasts can also differentiate into other cell types or enter a dormant state called quiescence. The process of quiescence in Drosophila neuroblasts is currently not well understood by scientists. Understanding how these cells switch between states is important for developing new stem cell therapies. When neuroblasts enter quiescence, the differentiation factor Prospero is transiently detected in the nucleus. This protein is briefly found at a low level during the transition to the dormant state. The entry into quiescence is followed by a unique molecular profile lacking most progenitor markers. A pulse of low level nuclear Prospero can drive proliferating larval neuroblasts into quiescence. This finding confirms that the presence of the protein is sufficient to trigger the dormant state. The study proposes that Prospero levels distinguish three progenitor fates for these brain stem cells. Different levels of Prospero act as a switch to determine the behavior of the neuroblast.

generated_summary: The biological world is homochiral and maintaining this homochirality is essential for cell survival. Homochirality means that cells use only one mirror-image form of molecules like amino acids. The enzyme D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase selectively removes D-amino acids mistakenly attached to tRNAs. This enzyme is also known as DTD and acts as a proofreading mechanism. The crystal structure of dimeric DTD from Plasmodium falciparum shows how the enzyme works. DTD uses a specific Gly-cisPro dipeptide to capture the chiral centre of incoming molecules. A side chain-independent mode of substrate recognition allows DTD to act on multiple D-amino acids. This recognition occurs even though no protein residues are directly involved in catalysis. Strict chiral specificity explains how the abundant cellular pool of L-aminoacyl-tRNAs escapes this step. The enzyme design ensures that only the incorrect D-form is targeted for removal. This study elucidates a chiral enforcement mechanism that prevents D-amino acid infiltration. This fundamental enantioselection process was crucial during the evolution of the translational apparatus. The lack of recognition of side chain atoms treats different amino acids alike. This binding pocket is a perfect fit for the shared chiral center. The structural design provides an elegant mechanism for rejecting L-chirality from the pocket. L-amino acids are excluded regardless of their specific chemical side chains.

feedback_items.source_span: The crystal structure of dimeric D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase ( DTD ) from Plasmodium falciparum in complex with a substrate-mimicking analog shows how it uses an invariant ‘cross-subunit’ Gly-cisPro dipeptide to capture the chiral centre of incoming D-aminoacyl-tRNA . The crystal structure of dimeric D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase ( DTD ) from Plasmodium falciparum in complex with a substrate-mimicking analog shows how it uses an invariant ‘cross-subunit’ Gly-cisPro dipeptide to capture the chiral centre of incoming D-aminoacyl-tRNA . In this study , we report the mechanism of this crucial process with the help of high resolution structures of PfDTD in complex with a substrate-mimicking analog .

options.C: The crystal structure of dimeric D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) from Homo sapiens, in complex with a substrate-mimicking analog, reveals that DTD uses an invariant 'cross-subunit' Gly-cisPro dipeptide to capture the chiral center of incoming D-aminoacyl-tRNA.

generated_summary: The CFTR protein is a channel that allows chloride to pass through cells. ATP-binding-induced dimerization of two nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) opens the pore. The molecular motions underlying spontaneous gating were previously unclear to researchers. It was unknown if NBDs still form dimers during these spontaneous events. This study correlates energetic coupling between residues with spontaneous pore opening. Researchers measured these interactions across the dimer interface in single CFTR channels. The findings provide insights for understanding CF mutation and drug mechanisms. This explains how drugs like ivacaftor affect both ATP-driven and spontaneous activity. The results clarify how phosphorylation and mutations influence channel activity. The study offers new insights into how cystic fibrosis treatments work. ATP acts as a molecular glue to stabilize the open state. The presence of bound ATP does not alter the global arrangement of conformations.

generated_summary: Researchers identified a powerful mechanism for the assembly and mobility of transmembrane proteins in lipid bilayers. This force is a pre-transition effect related to the transition between ordered and disordered membrane phases. Large-scale molecular simulation showed that a protein can stabilize a microscopic order-disorder interface. This occurs when the protein hydrophobic thickness matches the disordered phase within an ordered bilayer. When two proteins approach each other, they assemble to reduce the net interfacial energy. The tension of the interface pulls the two proteins together into a single group. The researchers named this phenomenon the orderphobic effect, which is analogous to the hydrophobic effect. The orderphobic effect leverages the power of a phase transition to drive protein interactions. The orderphobic effect is influenced by the proximity to the order-disorder phase transition. The strength and range of the orderphobic effect are significantly larger than membrane elasticity forces. This suggests the effect is a dominant force for protein assembly in the membranes studied.

Researchers used optical tweezers to observe four distinct stages of SNARE assembly. These stages involve the N-terminal, middle, C-terminal, and linker domains. Specific mutations in SNARE layers differentially affect how the proteins assemble. Some changes cause minor effects while others significantly alter the assembly speed. The N-terminal domain is responsible for docking vesicles to the membrane. The C-terminal domain drives the final fusion of the membranes together. The middle domain regulates both the assembly process and membrane fusion. Each part of the protein performs a unique task during neurotransmitter release. Munc18-1 initiates SNARE assembly and stabilizes a half-zippered protein complex. This stabilization requires a specific region called the N-terminal regulatory domain. SNARE domains have distinct functions that are closely chaperoned by Munc18-1. Munc18-1 acts on folding intermediates to guide the entire assembly process. The C-terminal domain acts as a power stroke to drive membrane fusion. The middle domain is essential for regulating the kinetics of this fusion.

generated_summary: Interpreting visual scenes typically requires people to accumulate information from multiple locations in a scene. Many situations require multiple fixations to extract several details at different locations to make a decision. Participants in a visual categorization task followed an active sensing strategy to choose their eye movements. This strategy incorporates information already acquired about the scene and knowledge of the statistical structure of patterns. The study used a novel gaze-contingent paradigm to track how people successively revealed small image apertures. This method allowed researchers to assess how participants actively chose where to look during the task. Categorization performance markedly improved when an optimal Bayesian active sensor algorithm revealed the locations to participants. The algorithm chose the next fixation location to maximally reduce uncertainty about the image category. A major portion of human suboptimality arises from prior biases, perceptual noise, and inaccuracies in eye movements. The central process of selecting fixation locations was found to be around 70% efficient in this task. Participants select eye movements with the goal of maximizing information about abstract categories. This process requires the integration of information from multiple locations to solve the task efficiently. The task required a closed-loop interaction between perception and the planning of each new eye movement. No single location was enough to solve the task without combining data from several different spots.

candidate_summaries.summary: Interpreting visual scenes typically requires people to accumulate information from multiple locations in a scene. Many situations require multiple fixations to extract several details at different locations to make a decision. Participants in a visual categorization task followed an active sensing strategy to choose their eye movements. This strategy incorporates information already acquired about the scene and knowledge of the statistical structure of patterns. The study used a novel gaze-contingent paradigm to track how people successively revealed small image apertures. This method allowed researchers to assess how participants actively chose where to look during the task. Categorization performance markedly improved when an optimal Bayesian active sensor algorithm revealed the locations to participants. The algorithm chose the next fixation location to maximally reduce uncertainty about the image category. A major portion of human suboptimality arises from prior biases, perceptual noise, and inaccuracies in eye movements. The central process of selecting fixation locations was found to be around 70% efficient in this task. Participants select eye movements with the goal of maximizing information about abstract categories. This process requires the integration of information from multiple locations to solve the task efficiently. The task required a closed-loop interaction between perception and the planning of each new eye movement. No single location was enough to solve the task without combining data from several different spots.

generated_summary: Cdc48 has a new function in the ubiquitin-dependent regulation of mitochondrial dynamics. Mitochondrial dynamics include the process of fusion where mitochondria combine. The deubiquitylases Ubp12 and Ubp2 have opposing effects on mitochondrial fusion. These enzymes cleave different ubiquitin chains on the mitofusin protein Fzo1. Cdc48 integrates the activities of Ubp12 and Ubp2 which are themselves ubiquitylated. This means Cdc48 acts as a central regulator for these two enzymes. Cdc48 promotes the proteolysis of Ubp12 to stabilize pro-fusion ubiquitylation on Fzo1. Proteolysis is the breakdown of proteins within the cell. Loss of Ubp12 stabilizes Ubp2 to facilitate removal of ubiquitin chains inhibiting fusion. This removal of specific chains on Fzo1 allows mitochondrial fusion to occur. Cdc48 synergistically regulates the ubiquitylation status of Fzo1 to control fusion balance. This control determines the activation or repression of mitochondrial fusion events. The study unravels a new cascade of ubiquitylation events involving Cdc48 and two DUBs. This cascade fine-tunes the fusogenic activity of the Fzo1 protein. Cdc48 is required to maintain the Fzo1 protein to promote fusion events. The protein Fzo1 is a key gatekeeper of the fusion mechanism. Cdc48 supports the degradation of Ubp12 in a proteasome-dependent manner. The proteasome is a cellular structure that breaks down unwanted proteins.

generated_summary: Cilia and flagella are assembled and maintained by a process called intraflagellar transport. This mechanism, known as IFT, involves more than 20 different proteins. The specific functions of individual IFT proteins are currently mostly unclear. Researchers need to understand how each protein contributes to the transport system. This study focused on a specific protein called TTC26/DYF13. Scientists suspected that TTC26/DYF13 was a part of the IFT machinery. TTC26/DYF13 is an IFT complex B protein in mammalian cells and algae. The researchers used live imaging and biochemical approaches to confirm this finding. Reducing this protein in zebrafish embryos resulted in short cilia with abnormal motility. Mutations in the algae C. reinhardtii also caused similar defects in movement. IFT particle assembly and speed were normal in the dyf13 mutant flagella. This result is different from what is seen in other complex B mutants. A specific set of motility-related proteins was depleted in the dyf13 mutant. Proteomic and biochemical analyses were used to identify these missing proteins. These results show that different IFT proteins are responsible for different cargo subsets. This finding helps explain the overall complexity of the IFT machinery.

generated_summary: Lymphatic invasion and lymph node metastasis correlate with poor clinical outcome in melanoma. Melanoma is an aggressive skin cancer that often spreads through the lymphatic system. The mechanisms of lymphatic dissemination in distant metastasis remain incompletely understood. Researchers want to know how cancer cells move from lymph vessels to distant organs. Exposure of human WM852 melanoma cells to lymphatic endothelial cells promotes distant organ metastasis. This interaction was studied using a 3D co-culture method and tested in mice. The metastatic melanoma cells adopted an invasively sprouting phenotype in a 3D matrix. This change in cell behavior depended on the proteins MMP14, Notch3, and β1-integrin. MMP14 was necessary for LEC-induced Notch3 induction and coincident β1-integrin activation. The protein MMP14 acts as a key upstream regulator to trigger these other proteins. MMP14 and Notch3 were required for LEC-mediated metastasis of zebrafish xenografts. Zebrafish models confirmed that these proteins are essential for the cancer to spread. This study uncovers a unique mechanism whereby LEC contact promotes melanoma metastasis. The contact induces a reversible switch from 3D growth to an invasively sprouting phenotype. Stromal lymphatic endothelium acts as a key trigger for tissue colonization at distant organs. Phenotype switching supports both hematogenous dissemination and colonization of new tissues.

generated_summary: Latent Epstein-Barr virus infection is linked to several types of human cancers. This virus can stay dormant in the body for a long time. The virus expresses oncogenes that promote cell growth and inhibit apoptotic response. Apoptosis is a natural process where damaged cells trigger their own death. The viral protein LMP1 is critical for the survival of immortalized B cells. LMP1 works by continuously activating a survival pathway called NFκB. During early infection, EBV induces rapid B cell proliferation with low LMP1 levels. These early-infected cells multiply quickly despite having very little apoptosis. The study aimed to define the mechanism of survival without high LMP1 levels. Researchers wanted to know how cells survive early after infection. The study used BH3 profiling to investigate mitochondrial regulation of apoptosis. The results showed a transition from BCL-2 to MCL-1 and BFL-1 proteins. This change in survival mechanisms relies on the viral EBNA3A protein. EBNA3A regulates MCL-1 mitochondrial localization and BFL-1 transcription. This study defines a new role for EBNA3A in the suppression of apoptosis. These findings have important implications for understanding EBV lymphomagenesis. Suppression of apoptosis by the virus is essential for establishing latent infection. This process also promotes tumor formation in hosts with suppressed immune systems.

generated_summary: Heterostyly is a widespread floral adaptation that promotes outbreeding in plants. This adaptation involves flowers having different arrangements of their reproductive organs. In Primula primroses, heterostyly is controlled by the S-locus supergene. The S-locus supergene determines the reciprocal arrangement of reproductive organs. The study identified the Primula CYP734A50 gene as the G locus. The CYP734A50 gene determines the style-length dimorphism in these flowers. The CYP734A50 gene encodes a putative brassinosteroid-degrading enzyme. Brassinosteroids are plant hormones that typically promote growth in tissues. The CYP734A50 gene is only present on the short-styled S-morph haplotype. This gene is specifically expressed in the styles of S-morph flowers. The loss or inactivation of CYP734A50 leads to long styles. This confirms the gene is necessary for maintaining short style lengths. The CYP734A50 gene arose by a duplication specific to the Primulaceae lineage. The gene also shows an accelerated rate of molecular evolution. The results provide a mechanistic explanation for the Primula style-length dimorphism. These findings shed light on the evolution of the S-locus supergene. The S-locus supergene also controls incompatibility between the two flower types. This genetic system prevents self-pollination between different flower morphs. The S-locus serves as a model for a complex plant supergene. The study clarifies how complex genetic clusters evolve in plants.

feedback_items.source_span: Depletion of Cep120 in quiescent mouse and human cells causes accumulation of pericentriolar material ( PCM ) components including pericentrin , Cdk5Rap2 , ninein and Cep170 . We noted a roughly 2-fold increase in pericentrin levels on the single daughter centriole when Cep120 was absent ( Figure 2—figure supplement 2F ) .

Hypoxia activates the Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier pathway in rat cerebellar granule neurons. This pathway is also called the SUMO pathway. Mutation of NaV1.2-Lys38 prevents both SUMOylation and the increase in INa. A deSUMOylating enzyme also prevents these changes from occurring. Hypoxia-induced linkage of SUMO1 to the channels is complete within 40 seconds. This rapid linkage shifts the voltage-dependence of channel activation. The shift in activation allows depolarizing steps to evoke larger sodium currents. Larger currents mean more sodium ions flow into the neurons. The SUMO pathway and NaV1.2 are potential targets for neuroprotective interventions. These targets are important because INa plays a role in hypoxic brain damage. Reducing damage from acute hypoxic insults may involve targeting these specific channels. Protecting central neurons is the main goal of these potential therapies. Neurons in the brain require a continuous supply of oxygen for normal activity. A lack of oxygen rapidly increases the flow of sodium ions into brain cells.

Mice lacking the TRAF2 protein usually die around the time of birth. This early death makes it difficult to study the protein in adult tissues. The specific role of the TRAF2 RING domain remains a controversial topic. Scientists disagree on how this specific part of the protein actually works. Some researchers suggested TRAF2 needs a lipid called S1P to function. The enzyme sphingosine kinase 1 produces this lipid to help TRAF2 work. Removing Traf2 from skin cells caused severe psoriatic skin inflammation in mice. However, a deficiency in the Sphk1 enzyme did not cause these skin problems. The loss of Traf2 disrupted important NF-κB and MAP kinase signaling pathways. This disruption led to the abnormal thickening of the outer skin layer. feedback_items.source_span: However , structural and in vitro analyses indicate that , unlike TRAF6 , the RING domain of TRAF2 is unable to bind E2 conjugating enzymes ( Yin et al . , 2009 ) , and is therefore unlikely to have intrinsic E3 ligase activity . Recently , it was suggested that the RING domain of TRAF2 requires S1P as a co-factor for its E3 ligase activity ( Alvarez et al . , 2010 ) . A potential resolution for this conundrum was proposed by Alvarez et al . who suggested that the RING of TRAF2 required a lipid co-factor , S1P , to function as an E3 ligase ( Alvarez et al . , 2010 ) .

generated_summary: Glucocorticoids are common drugs, but no biomarker exists to quantify their action. Doctors currently lack a reliable way to measure how these drugs work. The study aimed to identify and validate circulating biomarkers of glucocorticoid action. Researchers looked for markers in the blood that track drug activity. The study included 10 subjects with primary adrenal insufficiency during drug exposure. These patients do not produce their own glucocorticoids, allowing precise control. Integrated multi-omic analysis compared the transcriptome, miRNAomic, and serum metabolomics data. This method combines gene activity and metabolic products for a complete view. A transcriptomic profile from two tissues was predictive of glucocorticoid exposure. The profile used gene activity from blood cells and adipose tissue. A microRNA called miR-122-5p correlated with glucocorticoid-regulated genes and metabolites. MicroRNAs are small molecules that help control how genes are expressed. The identified miR-122-5p was replicated in independent studies with varying exposure. Testing in other groups confirms the molecule is a reliable indicator. These results help create biomarkers to individualize and optimize glucocorticoid therapy. Better markers could explain diseases like obesity and cardiovascular disease. New biomarkers help doctors tailor drug doses to each patient. Personalized dosing reduces side effects and improves treatment outcomes.

generated_summary: The global malaria burden has decreased over the last decade and many nations are attempting elimination. Many countries now aim to completely banish the disease within their borders. Asymptomatic malaria infections are not normally diagnosed or treated, posing a major hurdle for elimination efforts. People with asymptomatic malaria do not show symptoms but can still spread the parasite. Mass drug administration (MDA) is one solution, with success depending on adequate population participation. This method involves giving antimalarial drugs to everyone in a community at once. Researchers conducted a spatial and temporal analysis of malaria in four villages in Kayin State, Myanmar. The study tracked malaria episodes and asymptomatic infections in villages undergoing mass drug administration. Individuals from neighborhoods with low MDA adherence had 2.85 times the odds of having a malaria episode. This increased risk occurred regardless of whether the specific individual participated in the drug program. This study provides the first documentation of a herd effect for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. A herd effect means high community participation protects even those who did not take the medicine. High mosquito biting rates and living with someone with malaria were also predictors of clinical episodes. Having an asymptomatic malaria infection also predicted whether a person would develop a clinical episode. Spatial clustering of non-adherence to MDA may frustrate elimination efforts even with high overall participation. Small groups of people who do not participate can allow the disease to persist locally.

generated_summary: Ternatin is a natural product that kills cells and prevents fat formation. The molecular mode of action for this compound was previously unknown. New synthetic ternatin variants are cytotoxic toward cancer cells. These variants show up to 500-fold greater potency than ternatin itself. The translation elongation factor-1A ternary complex is a specific target of ternatin. This complex includes the eEF1A protein, GTP, and aminoacyl-tRNA molecules. Unrelated natural products like didemnin and cytotrienin also bind to this complex. These different compounds show competitive binding at the same molecular site. Mutations in domain III of eEF1A prevent ternatin from binding. These specific changes confer resistance to the cytotoxic effects of the drug. The adjacent hydrophobic surface is a functional hot spot for eEF1A modulation. This surface allows molecules to interact with and change the protein function. The eEF1A ternary complex is a common target for cytotoxic natural products. Many different cell-killing compounds have evolved to target this specific protein machinery. A ternatin photo-affinity probe helped identify the specific protein target. The probe crosslinked to the purified protein only within its ternary complex. Potent variants require a smaller dose to achieve the same effect. Lower doses of the compound are still able to kill cancer cells.

The study identified a novel regulatory axis involving FAK and PYK2 proteins. These proteins are also elevated in adenomas found in APCmin/+ mice. Phosphorylation of GSK3βY216 by FAK and PYK2 determines GSK3β recruitment of β-TrCP. GSK3β is a protein that normally switches the Wnt pathway off.

generated_summary: Tuberculous meningitis is a brain infection with high mortality linked to excessive inflammation. This severe condition involves swelling of the lining around the brain. Adjunctive anti-inflammatory corticosteroids reduce mortality in this disease by only 30%. This limited success suggests that inflammation causes only some of the deaths. A Vietnam study showed corticosteroid survival benefits were strongest with a specific LTA4H gene variant. The LTA4H gene helps regulate the balance of inflammatory signals in the body. Patients with the LTA4H TT genotype had increased survival when treated with these drugs. The TT genotype leads to higher gene expression and hyper-inflammatory responses. However, a study in Indonesia did not find this LTA4H TT genotype survival benefit. This difference between the two studies created a puzzle for researchers. New Bayesian methods show the LTA4H TT genotype confers survival benefit in both populations. This benefit begins early and continues long-term for patients in both countries. The survival benefit is nullified in the most severe cases with high early mortality. Extreme disease severity may override the advantages provided by the specific genotype. LTA4H genotyping and disease severity assessment may target therapy to patients who benefit most. This approach helps doctors avoid giving drugs to those unlikely to see clinical gains.

generated_summary: Inflammation is necessary for promoting and sustaining CD8+ T cell responses. These immune cells are essential for fighting various infections in the body. IRF-5 activates genes that encode key pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF. Cytokines are signaling proteins that help control the activity of immune cells. Mice lacking HIF-1α showed a higher frequency of short-lived effector cells. Short-lived effector cells are specialized immune cells that actively kill infected cells. Mice with targeted depletion of HIF-1α had a significantly lower splenic parasite burden. This suggests Leishmania parasites use HIF-1α to evade the immune system. Inducing HIF-1α allows Leishmania parasites to establish persistent infections in the host. Persistent infections are long-lasting and difficult for the immune system to clear.

The study confirmed all previously reported associations between expressed PfEMP1 sequences and severe disease. Confirming these known links strengthens the reliability of the new findings. These findings will inform efforts to identify new vaccine targets for severe malaria. Identifying specific protein segments helps researchers design more effective vaccines.

generated_summary: Toxoplasma is an obligate intracellular parasite that replicates within a specialized compartment in mammalian cells. This compartment is called the parasitophorous vacuole and does not fuse with other host organelles. This study examined how Toxoplasma exploits host lipid droplets which are fat storage organelles. Lipid droplets are common structures in cells that store essential fats and proteins. Toxoplasma replication is reduced in host cells that are depleted of these lipid droplets. Growth also slows when the host cannot break down fats through triacylglycerol lipolysis. Throughout infection the parasitophorous vacuole is surrounded by host lipid droplets. This close proximity allows the parasite to stay near its primary source of fat. Toxoplasma can access lipids stored in host droplets and incorporates them into its own membranes. The parasite also uses these salvaged fats to build its own internal storage droplets. Toxoplasma intercepts and internalizes host lipid droplets within the vacuole to access their lipids. These droplets become wrapped by an internal network of membranes inside the vacuole. Mutant parasites with an impaired membrane network show reduced lipid uptake from host droplets. This confirms that the internal membrane network is essential for gathering nutrients. Parasites lacking a specific enzyme are less efficient at salvaging lipids from host droplets. This enzyme helps process the droplets to release their lipid content for the parasite.

feedback_items.source_span: Recent interest in male-based sterile insect technique ( SIT ) and incompatible insect technique ( IIT ) to control Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus populations has revealed the need for an economical , rapid diagnostic tool for determining dispersion and mating success of sterilized males in the wild . generated_summary: Gene retroposition creates significant genetic variation among individuals. This process involves copying genetic material and inserting it into new locations. This study investigated the variation in loss of ancestral retrocopies among different human populations. Researchers used data from the 1000 Genomes Project to track these genetic changes. Retrocopy expression levels were examined using RNA-Seq data. The team used data from the Ilumina BodyMap project and the Geuvadis Consortium. The study detected 193 RDVs, mostly resulting from retrocopy deletion. These variations represent instances where a gene copy is present or absent. The expression of 11 ancestral retrogenes was experimentally confirmed. These specific genes were deleted in the genomes of some individuals. The deletion frequency for 10 of these 11 retrogenes is very low. A low frequency means these genes are rarely missing in the population. The expression and low rate of deletion suggest these 10 retrocopies have functionality. Functionality means these genes likely perform useful biological tasks. The study found 9 retrogenes with statistically significant differential expression between populations. This means the activity levels of these genes vary by geographic group.

generated_summary: Environmental insults like oxidative stress can damage cell membranes. This type of stress occurs when harmful molecules overwhelm the cell. Lysosomes are particularly sensitive to membrane permeabilization. These acidic compartments rely on stable proton gradients to function properly. Apolipoprotein D is an extracellular lipid binding protein with antioxidant capacity. This protein, also called ApoD, helps cells resist oxidative damage. The cellular mechanism by which ApoD provides protection is not yet understood. Researchers wanted to find how this protein preserves cell health. This study analyzed ApoD intracellular traffic during paraquat-induced oxidative stress. The team tracked how the protein moves inside the cell. ApoD is endocytosed and targeted to a subset of vulnerable lysosomes. The protein enters the cell and moves to specific damaged compartments. ApoD is necessary for lysosomes to recover from oxidation-induced alkalinization. This recovery occurs in both brain support cells and neurons. ApoD accomplishes its function by preventing lysosomal membrane permeabilization. The protein keeps the protective outer layer of the lysosome intact. The study identifies lipoprotein-mediated regulation of lysosomal membrane integrity as a new mechanism. This process is critical for the outcome of many neurodegenerative diseases.

generated_summary: The Dominican Republic experienced a Zika virus epidemic shortly after a large dengue epidemic. generated_summary: A measure called integrated information quantifies how a system generates more information than its individual parts. This measure, known as ΦDM, may reflect levels of consciousness generated by neural systems. The ΦDM measure is defined only for discrete Markov systems which are unusual in biology. This restriction means that the original measure can rarely be measured in practice for biological data. Researchers developed two new measures called ΦE and ΦAR to overcome these practical limitations. These new tools are easy to apply to time-series data from real biological systems. The new measures provide opportunities for examining information integration in real and model systems. These results carry implications for relations between integrated information, consciousness, and other neurocognitive processes. The findings pose challenges for theories that ascribe physical meaning to the measured quantities. This challenge specifically affects theories that treat integrated information as a fundamental physical quantity. The ΦE measure remains easy to measure because it uses empirical covariance matrices. This tool works for continuous or discrete stochastic systems without requiring system perturbation. A Markovian system is one where the future depends only on the present state. Complex biological systems are typically non-Markovian and are often measured as continuous data.

generated_summary: Pneumococcal meningitis is a common and severe bacterial infection of the brain. This infection is caused by the bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae. Individuals with pneumococcal meningitis experience selective synaptic loss in the frontal neocortex. Synapses are the essential connections that allow brain cells to communicate. In mouse astrocytes, pneumolysin initiated the release of glutamate in a calcium-dependent manner. Astrocytes are support cells in the brain that help regulate the environment. feedback_items.source_span: The NMDA glutamate receptor antagonists MK801 and D-AP5 reduced this pathology . Thus , we exposed acute mouse brain slices to 10 µM non-competitive NMDA inhibitor MK801 prior to the PLY challenge , and we observed a complete block of dendritic swelling formation ( Fig . 5A ) and a recovery of the number of dendritic spines in the neocortex ( Fig . 5B ) . generated_summary: The 5’-3’ decay is the primary mRNA decay pathway in many eukaryotes, including trypanosomes. This pathway is a crucial process that controls gene expression by breaking down messenger RNA. Trypanosomes lack homologues to all subunits of the conventional decapping complex found in other organisms. However, other parts of the decay process like deadenylation and 5’-3’ degradation are conserved. Trypanosomes use an ApaH-like phosphatase called ALPH1 as their major mRNA decapping enzyme. This enzyme fills a gap in understanding the unique mRNA decay pathway of these parasites. The RNAi depletion of ALPH1 is lethal to the parasites and causes massive mRNA accumulation. These accumulated mRNAs are deadenylated but have not yet started the 5’-3’ decay process. ALPH1 acts downstream of deadenylation and upstream of mRNA degradation during the decay process. generated_summary: Under nitrogen deprivation, Anabaena filaments develop a pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts separated by vegetative cells. These filaments consist of about ten photosynthetic cells between each specialized nitrogen-fixing cell. The coupling of gene expression fluctuations between cells along a multicellular filament was previously unknown. Researchers aimed to see if variations in gene activity were linked between neighboring cells. The study investigated HetR gene expression fluctuations using a chromosomally-encoded translational hetR-gfp fusion. HetR is a transcription factor essential for the differentiation of specialized heterocysts. Expression fluctuations of hetR in nearby cells are coupled within a range of two to three cells. This spatial range sets the scale for how cells interact along the filament. Correlations between cells predominantly arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division. Molecules moving between cells create stronger links than the process of cells splitting. Fluctuations in hetR expression after nitrogen step-down can build up on those under nitrogen-replete conditions. The developmental changes rely on patterns already present when nitrogen is abundant. The HetR inhibitor PatS and septal protein SepJ are essential determinants of hetR expression fluctuations. Positive HetR auto-regulation also helps control how these fluctuations are distributed along filaments. Proteins for activation and inhibition combine with gene expression stochasticity to control the developmental pattern. These factors work together to create the organized one-dimensional pattern seen in Anabaena.

Participants performed a rapid target-pointing task where the offset between visual feedback and movement end-points was manipulated. This manipulation changed the expected location of the target relative to the actual hand movement. The visual feedback had horizontal offsets that varied based on the target's shape. Different shapes required different pointing adjustments to successfully hit the target. The target shapes were part of a continuous set, morphed between spiky and circular forms. This allowed researchers to test how people react to shapes that fall between the trained examples. After training, participants' performance was tested on novel target shapes, without feedback. Testing without feedback shows what the participants actually learned during the training phase. Learning the associations required explicit awareness of the cues' role, consistent with the Bayesian learning model. Participants applied the mapping of the trained shape most similar to the current one. The Bayesian learning model predicted that learning would slow down with more training pairs. Experimental results confirmed that increasing the number of shapes made the learning process slower. The good correspondence between the Bayesian learning model and empirical results suggests a possible mechanism for learning. This model explains how the brain manages simultaneously learning multiple visuomotor mappings.

generated_summary: Aedes aegypti is the primary mosquito vector for dengue, which is a major global arboviral infection. Dengue is a viral disease spread to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Controlling Aedes aegypti populations is the main method for preventing dengue transmission until a vaccine is available. Reducing the number of mosquitoes helps stop the virus from spreading between people. Accurate predictions of vector populations are necessary to evaluate control methods and population reduction strategies. Knowing where mosquitoes live helps health officials plan better ways to eliminate them. Most previous studies on Aedes aegypti populations have not considered the spatial density of larval development sites. Spatial density refers to how close together different mosquito breeding locations are in an area. The study data came from pupal surveys conducted in rural Kamphaeng Phet, Thailand, from 2004 to 2007. Researchers counted mosquito pupae in water containers over this four-year period. Regression modeling was used to assess the effect of larval development site density and seasonal variation. The model also examined how access to piped water influenced the number of mosquitoes produced. The number and density of suitable larval development sites were the primary factors determining mosquito abundance. These factors influenced both the distribution and the total count of Aedes aegypti pupae. The productivity of most container types increased significantly as the habitat density increased. Individual containers produced more mosquitoes when they were located near many other breeding sites.

generated_summary: In fungal cells, cytokinesis requires the coordinated closure of a contractile actomyosin ring (CAR). This process also requires the synthesis of a special cell wall structure called the division septum. The mechanism by which CAR proteins interact with septum synthesis enzymes remains unclear. Researchers aim to understand how these molecules work together to form the division septum. Cooperation between the protein Pxl1 and the enzyme Bgs1 is required for stable CAR anchorage. This cooperation ensures the ring attaches to the plasma membrane before the cleavage furrow forms. Lack of Pxl1 combined with Bgs1 depletion causes failure of ring contraction in fission yeast. This combination leads to abnormal cell wall overgrowth without the formation of a proper septum. Pxl1 concentration at the CAR increases during cytokinesis depending on the F-BAR protein Cdc15. Specifically, this increase in Pxl1 levels requires the SH3 domain of the Cdc15 protein. Bgs1 depletion in cells with a defective cdc15ΔSH3 allele causes ring disassembly and septation blockage. These defects are similar to the results seen in cells that completely lack Pxl1. The absence of Pxl1 is lethal when the function of the Cdc15 protein is affected. This lethal state causes the CAR to slide and deposit septum material along the cortex. CAR anchorage to the plasma membrane through Cdc15 and Pxl1 is necessary for CAR maintenance. Simultaneous Bgs1 activity is also essential for proper septum formation in fission yeast.

generated_summary: The intracellular parasite Toxoplasma possesses a gene for a protein containing a sterol-sensing domain. This sterol-sensing domain is a conserved part of proteins that regulate cholesterol levels. This protein is predicted to be a Niemann-Pick, type C1-related protein called NPC1. The protein contains many residues that are linked to human NPC disease. The researchers named this specific parasite protein TgNCR1. Naming the protein allows scientists to distinguish it from similar human proteins. TgNCR1 lacks endosomal targeting signals and localizes to flattened vesicles near the plasma membrane. The plasma membrane is the outer layer that protects the Toxoplasma cell. TgNCR1 restores cholesterol and GM1 clearance when placed in mammalian NPC1 mutant cells. This test confirms the protein can move lipids when targeted to the correct location. The researchers genetically disrupted NCR1 in Toxoplasma to create viable mutant parasites. These viable mutants allow scientists to study how the parasite functions without the protein. The ΔNCR1 strain shows normal cholesterol levels but an overaccumulation of other lipids. These lipids include cholesteryl esters, sphingomyelins, and ceramides stored in abundant lipid bodies. The ΔNCR1 mutant Toxoplasma can generate multiple daughters per mother cell at high frequencies. This change allows for fast replication and makes the parasite slightly more virulent.
